bull_bear.body:
- Integrated generation-cum-distribution model in Kolkata — own thermal plants (BBGS, Garden Reach) plus 100%-subsidiary Haldia (HEL) under a long-term PPA — reducing power-procurement risk.
- HEL ranked 1st in PLF-wise all-India ranking for thermal generating stations per the CEA report for 2025-26, evidencing generation efficiency.
- Diversified distribution footprint beyond Kolkata (NPCL Greater Noida, Chandigarh licence, Rajasthan and Maharashtra franchisees) reducing single-licence concentration.
- High digital collection efficiency — digital channels accounted for over 88% of bill payments and over 94% of overall revenue collection by March 2026.
- Early-mover renewable energy platform (Purvah Green Power) targeting 10 GW by 2031-32, diversifying growth beyond regulated Kolkata distribution.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geopolitical and commodity-price risk — The war in the Middle East has driven a surge in global energy prices which can spiral into broader inflation and dent confidence/investment, posing downside risk to India's growth outlook; separately, coal availability, price, quality and linkages for new projects continue to be issues of concern for CESC's thermal fleet.
- Power market structural risk (surplus capacity / PPA execution) — Industry-wide surplus power generation capacity exposes the sector — and CESC — to risks of difficulty executing PPAs and adverse price movements in the short-term power market.
- Ageing thermal generation asset risk — As CESC's power plants age, their operating efficiencies reduce; beyond a point, shutting down and replacing these plants becomes imperative, an operational and capital-intensity risk.
- Natural and man-made disaster risk — Nor'wester storms, cyclone, deluge, earthquake and fire can affect the Company's ability to supply quality, reliable power to its customers, requiring a standing three-layer disaster-management framework.
- Grid-integration and system-stability risk — Integrating renewable energy into the grid and scheduling through open-access power transactions increases variability in managing grid stability and demand-supply balance, a growing operational risk as CESC scales its RE portfolio.
- Regulatory and environmental-compliance risk — Power is a highly regulated sector; tightening environmental norms — efficient fly-ash management, mandatory Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD) installation at existing thermal plants, renewable purchase obligations, and mandated biomass co-firing — can make new project execution harder and raise operating costs.
- Geographic and licence concentration risk — Core generation-and-distribution operations remain concentrated in the licensed Kolkata, Howrah, Hooghly, North and South 24 Parganas area of West Bengal; distribution ventures outside Kolkata (Greater Noida, Rajasthan franchisees, Malegaon, Chandigarh) and independent generation projects are comparatively newer and smaller, so the core cash flow base is tied to a single state's regulatory and demand environment.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: CESC Limited is an integrated power utility engaged in generation and distribution of electricity across a 567 sq km licensed area — Kolkata, Howrah, Hooghly, and North & South 24 Parganas in West Bengal — supplying 3.78 million customers. Through subsidiaries it also runs independent thermal and renewable generation projects (Haldia, Dhariwal, Asansol, Crescent Power, Purvah) and distribution ventures outside Kolkata, including Noida Power Company Limited (Greater Noida), Chandigarh Power Distribution Limited, and distribution franchisees in Kota, Bharatpur, Bikaner (Rajasthan) and Malegaon (Maharashtra).

- HEL ranked 1st in PLF-wise all-India ranking for thermal generating stations per the CEA report for 2025-26, evidencing generation efficiency.
- Diversified distribution footprint beyond Kolkata (NPCL Greater Noida, Chandigarh licence, Rajasthan and Maharashtra franchisees) reducing single-licence concentration.
- High digital collection efficiency — digital channels accounted for over 88% of bill payments and over 94% of overall revenue collection by March 2026.

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Well laid-out strategy for growth via independent generation projects, including a recent foray into the renewable energy (RE) business with a target capacity of 10 GW by 2031-32 through a mix of solar, wind and hybrid projects, executed through dedicated subsidiary Purvah Green Power Private Limited.
- Continue to operate and grow distribution businesses outside Kolkata (Greater Noida via NPCL, Chandigarh, and franchisees in Kota, Bharatpur, Bikaner and Malegaon) as a growth avenue distinct from the core Kolkata licence.
- Ensuring uninterrupted supply of electricity while maintaining high service levels continues to be the overarching objective, with efficiency initiatives across Generation, Distribution and Customer Service.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: CESC's expansion is anchored in the renewable energy (RE) platform Purvah Green Power Private Limited, targeting a planned RE capacity of 3.2 GW by 2028-29 (Phase 1) and an overall 10 GW by 2031-32 (Phase 2) across solar, wind, hybrid and battery energy storage projects, backed by a development pipeline of approximately 8.4 GW of grid connectivity across the CTU and STU networks in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. At the end of FY2025-26, six RE projects with cumulative capacity of 2,400 MW were under implementation through Purvah's subsidiaries, won under competitive bidding: (i) 300 MW solar at Bhadla, Rajasthan (awarded by CESC; 296 MW already commissioned), (ii) 450 MW hybrid — 150 MW solar at Bikaner, Rajasthan plus 300 MW wind at Ananthapuram, Andhra Pradesh (awarded by NPCL), (iii) 300 MW solar with 180 MW/901 MWh BESS at Nagaur plus 250 MW wind at Bellary, Karnataka (awarded by REMCL for round-the-clock power to Indian Railways), (iv) 400 MW solar with 150 MW/600 MWh BESS at Bikaner, Rajasthan (awarded by SECI), (v) 250 MW wind at Bijapur, Karnataka (awarded by SECI), and (vi) a further hybrid project (details truncated in source). On the thermal side, independent generation capacity comprises the 2x300 MW Chandrapur/Chandanpur plant in Maharashtra under 100%-subsidiary Dhariwal Infrastructure Limited (DIL) — Unit-I sells under medium-term PPAs to Adani Electricity Mumbai, Tata Power and NPCL (225 MW aggregate) plus a new medium-term PPA with Maharashtra Airport Development Company for 10 MW starting April 2026; Unit-II sells under long-term PPAs, 100 MW to Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation and 171 MW to NPCL — and the 40 MW Asansol AFBC plant and 18 MW DC Ramanathapuram solar project, both under subsidiary Crescent Power Limited. On the Kolkata distribution network, the Company added 380 MVA of transformation capacity during the year (with a further 80 MVA unlocked via network reorganisation), commissioned three new 33/11-6 kV distribution stations (Birati South, Mukundapur, Mahesh D/S), commissioned a 500 MVA 400/220 kV power transformer at PGCIL's Subhasgram substation (at CESC's cost, deposit-work mode), continued standardising to higher-rated UG cables, and is installing a grid-connected 40 MW/80 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at one substation while contemplating further grid-connected BESS projects at strategic locations.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's electricity demand is expected to keep rising, driven by appliances/air-conditioning, electrified heating, electric mobility, advanced manufacturing, data centres and AI, with generation capacity growing faster than total energy demand as the economy electrifies.
- CESC's own Kolkata system demand was subdued in FY2025-26, particularly in Q1, due to a milder summer suppressing cooling-driven peak demand, though full-year system demand remained broadly stable versus the prior year.
- A structural shift in the global and Indian energy mix toward renewable technologies (led by solar PV, with growing interest in nuclear) is underway, supporting the rationale for CESC's RE expansion through Purvah.
- Global energy markets were disrupted by the Middle East conflict from end-February 2026 (Strait of Hormuz transit risk), pushing commodity and energy prices higher into 2026, a cost/macro backdrop management flags alongside India's resilient GDP growth (7.6% in FY2025-26).
- Distribution ventures outside Kolkata are a growth driver: the six operational ventures collectively serviced about 11.4 lakh consumers and grew electricity sales 26% year-on-year to 8,983 million units in FY2025-26.
- 2,400 MW of renewable energy projects were under implementation across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh through subsidiaries as at end of FY2025-26, representing the near-term RE project pipeline; 296 MW of this had been commissioned since the close of the year.
